Tun discuesion of the Resolutions proposed by Mr. (Redstone will probably terminate while our present issue Is passing through the press, and it is not therefore within our power to announce the result of the division which will probably be taken in the House of Commons during the small hours of Satur- day morning. But as there is many a story I which is of more interest to the readers. a I narrative of events than any outcome or de- nouement to which they can possibly lead, so I here se may find more that concerns us in looking over the speeches which have been delivered, than any effect which that sum- . . . . ..„ .

pound of insincerity, al will and ignorance, which goes to make up the Tory party, may produce in refusing to accept the Itesolutions proposed by Mr. Uladstone as a declaration of the principles which guide the policy of

England. • Our friend, or at least our neighbour Mr. Croas, the Home Secretary, is credited with having made the moat successful speech on the Ministerial side. ()utsp..ken, it is called, and if not dignitied, generous and straight forward. This may be all very well, and we do not wish in the least to detract from any praise, to which Mr. Cross may be entitled, but at the same time we cannot but remem- ber that it is quite impossible for any man in the Home Secretary's position to speak for himself alone, since' none of Her Majesty's Minister., he is ee the philosophers would say, limited by the conditions of his environ-

went. How does it look for inetance, read by the fierce light of that blazing torch, which ' Lord Derby has just held up to Russia I And again, how would it compare with the bellicose eentimente of Lord Beaconsfield, or even for the neoretary for War? It is

iec—t7l-y irreconcilable w' ith them. The Ministry say, generally, that they cannot accept these resolutions, not because they are not true, but because they will not admit anything coming from an outsider or a foe, and because they have all along been engaged in the maintenance of peace and the protection of British interests. What's done says Burns, we partly make complete. Row they have bucceeded in preserving peace is' unfortunately plain enough, and if British interests are to be equally safe in their I hands, why then the Lord deliver as from . the Beaconsfield Cabinet. The main reason why the Government have been so uneuccessful in their aims is clearly traceable to their divided counsels. they started with every chance in their! favour, as Mr. Lowe said in his speech of I Tuesday last, but their want of success I was clearly traceable to the fact that they had at least three policies going on at the same time. The tiret of these three policies was that of systematic friendehip for Turkey and pernistent hostility towards Russia • that was the policy of the Prime ELlA- ter. In the second place, there was the policy which consisted in doing as little in could possibly be done, and when anything had to be done, then of doing that which was calculated to lessen its effect, all the while favouring Turkey as against Russia, and that was the policy of Lord Derby, the Secretary for Foreign Affairs. In the third place, there was the policy very eirailar to that which was tntertamed generally by the Liberal party, and that was the policy of the Marquie of alisbury, and the conduct id the Government varied just as those three poll. cies either in or out ot their turn came to the top. And besides this three-sided, this pris- matic policy which received and distorted the facts as they happened, there was a sys- tem of concealment carried on, a keeping back of the knowledge of what they were doing from the public that hal really proved injurious to the Ministry's own interests. For instance, after the Bulgarian atroci- ties became known, and the whole country rose as by a spontaneous movement, Lord Derby wrote his despatch of the 21st Sep- tember, in which he hotly denounced the crimes there committed; but this despatch was carefully concealed till long afterwards; and Lord Derby received deputation after deputation without giving them the slightest season to suppose that the cordial sympa- thies of the Government were with the time of these atrocities.
